source.title: Not All Explanations for Deep Learning Phenomena Are Equally Valuable
source.authors: Alan Jeffares; M. van der Schaar

record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that grokking is an edge-case phenomenon with limited practical relevance and that its study should be framed around broader explanatory value. It does not report a new test of the claim; its discussion relies on cited work.
record.gate_note: The paper describes grokking and summarizes findings from prior studies, but those cited results are not rows. Its own prime-count illustration measures a post-hoc quantity against test performance; it does not test the delayed-generalization timing, dataset-size dependence, mechanisms, or realistic-training claims in the versions.
record.test_reason: This is a position paper. Its statements on grokking's scope argue that V4 is not seen in practice and that V3 needs inflated initialization. Both rest entirely on cited work (Dziri et al., Liu et al. 2022b, Varma et al., Kumar et al., Prieto et al.), not on the paper's own results. Its one experiment, the prime-count illustration in Figure 4, is a deliberately absurd post-hoc metric. It is used to make a methodological point and does not measure delay timing, dataset-size dependence, mechanism, regime or realistic training. With no own results on any version, it neither tests nor uses the claim. I chose T6 over the reader's T5 because T5 would make it a test, and every argument here is citation-based.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors argue that grokking, double descent and lottery tickets are edge-case phenomena that rarely appear in practical settings. They say research on them should refine broad explanatory theories rather than narrow ad hoc hypotheses, and they call for pragmatic, utility-aware and more rigorous scientific practice.
record.recipe_differences: No reproduction or direct test of the original grokking method; the paper includes an illustrative prime-count analysis using the setting of Power et al. (2022).
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes, based on cited work, that grokking’s apparent extent can depend on dataset size, initialization scale, data encoding, and choice of metric; these are not tested here.

fits_no_version.finding: In the Power et al. grokking setting, the count of rounded prime-valued parameters tracks test accuracy. The authors explain this as an artifact of parameter magnitudes growing during training. Results are averaged over 10 seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc parameter statistics confounded with weight-magnitude growth can track grokking test-accuracy curves without explanatory value.

record.problems: The paper reports no new empirical test of the claim. Its statements about practical relevance and other grokking settings rely on cited work. The one illustrative result is described as an artifact and does not measure the claim's defining training/test timing.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The double-descent prime-count illustration is outside the claim's subject.

untested.parts: All: no own measurement of train/test timing or of delay vs training-set size; only cites Liu et al. 2022a that the effect weakens with larger datasets.
All: progress measures and circuit formation cited (Nanda et al.) only.
All: init-scale induction and non-algorithmic grokking discussed via Liu et al. 2022b and Varma et al. only.
All: asserts realistic grokking attempts unsuccessful, citing Dziri et al.; no own LLM test.
All: softmax numerical instability (Prieto et al.) and metric choice (Kumar et al.) mentioned via citation only.

record.verdict_notes: The ICML 2025 position paper's practical-irrelevance arguments (grokking limited to small algorithmic data, induced on other modalities only by large initialization, absent in realistic settings, partly a metric artifact) relate to V3, V4 and V7. They are summaries of cited studies, which should be assessed in their own right. Changed the tranche from T5 to T6 because the paper has no own evidence.

versions.untested_parts: The paper describes the phenomenon and cites prior work, but does not test training/test accuracy timing or how delay changes with training-set size.
Gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, and progress measures are discussed through citations, not tested.
Non-algorithmic data and initialization-scale or weight-norm effects are discussed through cited work, not tested.
The paper states that attempts to observe standard grokking in realistic scenarios have been unsuccessful, citing prior work; it reports no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning test of its own.
Efficiency accounts, critical dataset size, and ungrokking are not tested.
The paper does not test whether runs converge to the same algorithm.
Numerical softmax instability is mentioned as prior work; the paper does not test whether optimizer or numerical choices produce the delay.

conditions.value: Grokking experiment based on Power et al. (2022)

rows.measure: Whether the prime-parameter count tracks test performance
rows.value: The metric accurately tracks test performance.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged over 10 seeds; standard deviation displayed.
rows.locator: Figure 4; Appendix A, Additional Note on Prime Numbers Example
rows.note: This is an illustrative post-hoc metric, not a test of the versions' claims about grokking dynamics. The appendix attributes the tracking to parameter-magnitude confounding.
rows.check: The row is correctly unlinked. The measure is a prime-parameter count that the authors themselves attribute to a confound (parameter magnitude), not a grokking property. Figure 4 also appears to show a reproduced grokking curve in the Power et al. setting. That curve is a reproduction of the original, no numbers are given in the text, and it is illustrative only.

tranche.reason: Section 2.2 specifically argues against grokking's occurrence in realistic scenarios, bearing on V4. T5 includes specific arguments that a version needs qualifying; new experiments are not required for that classification.
